Selection for Evolutionary Algorithms

ABSTRACT
Adaptive Operator Selection (AOS) is a strategy in Evolutionary Al-
gorithms (EAs) that dynamically adjusts the application frequency
of operators to enhance search efficiency based on online perfor-
mance feedback. This paper introduces LAOS, an AOS framework
driven by Large Language Models (LLMs). We design a meta-prompt
to provide optimization state information (such as optimization
progress, best fitness, and population diversity) and operator credit
assignment, assisting LLMs in making adaptive decisions. Further-
more, LAOS maintains a dual-layer replay buffer structure: the of-
fline layer records historical experiences under fixed operator strate-
gies, while the online layer accumulates dynamically generated
experiences during execution. By employing a similar experience
sampling strategy, the framework can provide decision-making
support for LLMs, enhancing both the efficiency and accuracy of
search strategies. Experimental results on continuous numerical
optimization and three categories of combinatorial optimization
problems validate the effectiveness and generalization capability of
LAOS. This study demonstrates the feasibility of leveraging LLMs
for AOS, showcasing their potential in enhancing optimization
performance and supporting automated algorithm design.

1
INTRODUCTION
Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) have been widely applied to opti-
mization and decision-making problems across various fields, in-
cluding engineering [50], industry [40], economics [48], and bioin-
formatics [41], due to their capacity to yield high-quality solutions
within computationally feasible time frames. Although EAs gener-
ally follow a unified optimization framework, their performance
is heavily influenced by parameter settings such as the selection
and application rate of crossover and mutation operators [2]. Con-
sequently, the effective configuration and optimization of these
parameters have become a critical research topic. The issue of pa-
rameter settings can be categorized into two classes: parameter
tuning and parameter control [15].
Parameter tuning refers to the process of setting fixed parameter
values for an algorithm before its application to a specific problem,
with no further adjustments during optimization. Conventional
tuning methods, such as Iterated F-Race [6], ParamILS [25], Meta-
EAs [35], and HORA [4], typically achieve iterative refinement
by repeatedly performing generate-and-evaluate cycles and have
been widely adopted in practice [23]. However, empirical studies
suggest that fixed parameter configurations may fail to maintain
optimal performance throughout the optimization process, as differ-
ent stages may require distinct configurations [18, 21]. For instance,
Cervantes and Stephens demonstrated that any fixed mutation rate
may result in suboptimal trade-offs between exploration and ex-
ploitation [8]. Therefore, it is necessary to introduce parameter
control methods to dynamically adjust parameter settings during
the optimization of EAs to adapt to the evolving algorithmic needs.
Adaptive Operator Selection (AOS) is a critical component of
parameter control in EAs, facilitating dynamic operator selection by
adapting to the dynamic search landscape. Existing AOS methodolo-
gies can be categorized into two classes: stateless methods and state-
based methods [43, 44]. Stateless methods are straightforward to
implement, requiring no prior training, and typically employ mech-
anisms such as Probability Matching (PM) [52] or Multi-Armed
Bandit (MAB) models [12] to guide operator selection. However,
their lack of consideration for contextual information from the
optimization process may lead to suboptimal decisions. In contrast,
state-based methods formulate operator selection as a Markov De-
cision Process (MDP), leveraging reinforcement learning [14, 19]
to map optimization states to operator actions, thereby enhancing
adaptability. Despite their efficacy, these approaches often require
substantial training resources, leading to prohibitive computational
overhead. Thus, there is a compelling need to develop training-free
AOS strategies capable of effectively exploiting optimization con-
text. The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) [9, 27, 63]

presents novel avenues to address this challenge, signalling a po-
tential paradigm shift for AOS methodologies.
The development of LLMs has revolutionized artificial intelli-
gence, impacting diverse fields including natural language process-
ing [37], programming [53], and even integrated circuit design [7].
Beyond simply understanding natural language instructions, LLMs
excel at recognizing patterns from contextual demonstrations, en-
abling dynamic adaptation to a diverse range of tasks [54]. Yang et
al. [57] pioneered this paradigm by introducing Optimization by
Prompting (OPRO), leveraging LLM-generated optimization trajec-
tories to discover novel solutions. Building on this, Huang et al. [24]
integrated visual information, creating a multimodal LLM-powered
optimization framework that demonstrated a significant improve-
ment in solution quality for Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problems
(CVRPs). Liu et al. [33] further advanced the field with LLM-driven
EAs (LMEA), where the LLM guides parent selection, crossover,
and mutation, achieving faster convergence on Traveling Salesman
Problems (TSPs). Custode et al. [11]then applied LLMs for adaptive
step size control in (1 + 1)-ES, pioneering the application of LLMs
in the parameter control of EAs. Despite these advancements, the
application of LLMs to adaptive operator selection in EAs remains
unexplored in existing literature.
In this study, we propose LAOS, a training-free framework syner-
gizing stateless and state-based methods for adaptive operator selec-
tion. Its core innovations include: encoding state-space features into
structured prompts to enable LLM-driven landscape perception; in-
tegrating a credit assignment mechanism that quantifies operators’
historical performance for interpretable decisions; and designing a
dual-layer replay buffer (offline fixed-strategy storage and online
dynamic accumulation) to mitigate prompt redundancy through
similarity-guided sampling. Experiments on real-valued and com-
binatorial optimization demonstrate LAOS’s superior convergence
speed and solution quality compared to conventional methods,
establishing a new paradigm for online adaptive optimization.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. First, Sec-
tion 2 reviews foundational AOS and LLM-driven optimization
research. Next, Section 3 details the LAOS framework. Section 4 val-
idates its effectiveness across numerical and combinatorial bench-
marks. Finally, Section 5 concludes with key contributions and
future directions.
2
RELATED WORK
2.1
Adaptive Operator Selection
The goal of AOS is to dynamically select evolutionary operators
to maximize optimization effectiveness. This approach can be cat-
egorized into two types: stateless and state-based AOS methods.
Stateless AOS methods do not rely on the current state information
of the optimization process; instead, they select operators based on
their historical performance. These methods typically involve two
key steps: Credit Assignment (CA) and Operator Selection Rule
(OSR). The CA step defines how to reward operators based on their
past search performance, while the OSR utilizes these rewards to
determine which operator should be applied next.
In the process of CA, rewards are generally determined by com-
paring the fitness of the new and previous solutions. For instance,
Whitacre et al. [55] employed the mean fitness improvement over
the most recent𝑊iterations as the rewards for operators. However,
Fialho et al. [17] argued that rare, substantial improvements hold
greater significance than continuous, small fitness enhancements,
thus advocating for a reward mechanism based on the maximum
fitness improvement achieved recently. Building on these studies,
Li et al. [30] proposed a classic CA method based on Fitness-Rate-
Rank (FRR), introducing a decay factor to encourage the allocation
of more rewards to the best-performing operators.
Based on the allocated rewards, OSR is responsible for recom-
mending appropriate operators for subsequent optimization pro-
cesses. Classical OSR methods can be broadly categorized into two
types: PM and MAB methods. PM methods resemble a roulette
wheel strategy, where operators are selected in proportion to their
assigned probabilities, potentially resulting in excessive selection of
underperforming operators. To address this issue, Adaptive Pursuit
(AP) strategies adopt a winner-takes-all approach, which partially
mitigates this limitation [52]. Related studies include [47], [61],
and [62]. On the other hand, MAB methods treat operator selection
as a trade-off between exploration and exploitation. A substan-
tial body of research has emerged based on the Upper Confidence
Bound (UCB) strategy [34, 39]. For instance, Fialho [16] proposed
the Rank-based MAB (RMAB), which uses rank-based credit assign-
ment outcomes to replace the empirical estimates in UCB. Building
on this concept, Li et al. [30] further extended the FRR-based MAB
and successfully applied it to multi-objective optimization tasks.
Unlike stateless methods, state-based AOS methods dynamically
adjust operator selection by leveraging optimization states. Early
studies primarily relied on traditional reinforcement learning tech-
niques. For instance, Pettinger and Everson [45] pioneered the use
of Q(𝜆)-learning to select operators for Genetic Algorithms (GAs),
demonstrating superior performance over standard GAs on TSPs.
Inspired by this work, Chen et al. [10] adopted the SARSA algo-
rithm for similar control tasks. With the rapid development of deep
learning, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has been introduced
into the AOS domain to enhance the flexibility and adaptability
of operator selection. By integrating deep neural networks with
reinforcement learning algorithms, DRL methods effectively handle
high-dimensional continuous state spaces, enabling more precise
dynamic control in complex optimization problems. For example,
Sharma et al. [49] employed Double Deep Q-Network (DDQN) to
select mutation operators in Differential Evolution (DE), while Yi et
al. [59] used the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm to
choose components for metaheuristic algorithms, both achieving
better performance than traditional Q-learning methods. Addition-
ally, studies such as [38] and [60] further explored the applications
of DQN and Dueling DQN in AOS, highlighting the potential of
DRL approaches to enhance optimization performance.
2.2
LLMs for Optimization
Large language models, with their robust capabilities in contex-
tual understanding and reasoning, provide innovative insights and
methodologies for the optimization process. Based on the differ-
ent roles and functions of LLMs in the optimization process, this
study categorizes LLM-assisted optimization into three main types:
problem-driven LLM-based optimization, low-level LLM-assisted
EAs, and high-level LLM-assisted EAs.

Problem-driven LLM-based optimization refers to the direct gen-
eration of solutions for optimization problems by LLMs based on
textual descriptions of the problems. The OPRO framework, intro-
duced by Yang et al. [57], represents the first approach that utilizes
LLMs for non-gradient optimization problems. This method itera-
tively refines solutions by providing the LLM with problem descrip-
tions and optimization trajectories. Subsequently, this framework
has been employed across various optimization fields; for instance,
Li et al. [29] applied it to multi-objective optimization in Unmanned
Aerial Vehicle (UAV) networks, while Huang et al. [23] extended
it to multimodal optimization by integrating visual information.
However, some studies suggest that despite the potential of LLMs
for non-gradient optimization tasks, their direct application often
yields suboptimal performance due to the absence of distinctive
characteristics typical of traditional optimization methods [22].
Evolutionary algorithms typically follow a similar framework,
where using LLMs to drive specific components, such as crossover
and mutation operations, parameter control, and operator selection,
is referred to as low-level LLM-assisted EAs. Liu et al. [33] proposed
the LMEA framework, where LLMs perform crossover, mutation,
and solution selection during optimization. Meyerson et al. [36]
introduced Language Model Crossover (LMX), a model that utilizes
LLMs as operators for evolutionary mutation, applied in fields such
as symbolic regression and image generation. Similar efforts, such
as NSGA-II-LLM [33], focus on leveraging LLMs to assist NSGA-II
in performing crossover and mutation operations. In parameter
control, Custode et al. [11] employed LLMs to dynamically adjust
step sizes in the (1 + 1)-ES algorithm, balancing exploration and
exploitation throughout the optimization process.
High-level LLM-assisted EAs focus on algorithm selection and
generation rather than adjusting the internal components of algo-
rithms. For algorithm selection, Wu et al. [56] extracted algorithm
features from code using LLMs and match them with problem re-
quirements to select the most suitable algorithm. For algorithm
generation, Pluhacek et al. [46] employed LLMs to enumerate can-
didate algorithms fitting specific problems and generate algorithms
directly based on their features. Similar studies have been conducted
on mixed integer linear programming [1] and metaheuristic algo-
rithms [64]. Building on these foundations, Ye et al. [58] developed
the Language Hyper-Heuristics (LHHs) framework, introducing a
reflective evolutionary mechanism that provides linguistic gradi-
ents within the heuristic space. Additionally, Liu et al. [32] proposed
the Algorithm Evolution using LLMs (AEL) framework, treating
heuristic strategies as independent evolutionary entities optimized
collaboratively with code.

3.1
Algorithm Framework
In this study, we propose a novel LLM-driven AOS (LAOS) frame-
work to enhance the optimization efficiency of EAs. The detailed
implementation is presented in Algorithm 1. The algorithm begins
by initializing key parameters, including the number of iterations
𝑇, population size 𝑁, and the operator set 𝑆= {𝑠1, · · · ,𝑠𝐾}. Subse-
quently, a preliminary optimization phase is conducted using fixed
operators, and the resulting optimization experiences are stored in
the offline layer of the replay buffer (lines 2-7).
Following this initialization, the framework transitions to the
LLM-driven adaptive optimization phase. During this phase, opti-
mization experiences are stored in the online layer of the experience
pool (lines 9-12). The algorithm also calculates the optimization
state and applies the FRR strategy to assign credit to operators
(lines 13, 14). Additionally, LAOS retrieves similar historical expe-
riences from the replay buffer using a similarity-based sampling
mechanism, constructing a comprehensive meta-prompt that in-
corporates these insights (lines 15-19). Then, the LLM utilizes this
meta-prompt to select the most suitable operator for the next phase
of optimization while providing explanations for its selection (line
20). Finally, the LAOS framework terminates upon reaching the
predefined number of generations and returns the best solution.

3.2
Meta-Prompt Construction
Large Language Models possess the ability to identify patterns from
in-context examples, which paves the way for their application in
optimization tasks. Leveraging this potential, Yang et al. [57] formu-
lated optimization trajectories as meta-prompts to guide LLMs in
solving a variety of optimization problems. However, their research
also highlights a significant limitation: when LLMs are directly em-
ployed as optimizers for numerical or combinatorial optimization
problems, their performance often falls short of traditional optimiza-
tion algorithms. Custode et al. [11] further explored this approach,
similarly using optimization trajectories as meta-prompts to guide
LLMs in adjusting the step size of (1 + 1)-ES. Their experimental
results reveal that LLMs tend to gradually shrink the step size dur-
ing the optimization process, leading to challenges in achieving
an appropriate balance between exploration and exploitation. We
attribute this issue to the design of the meta-prompt. Providing the
full optimization trajectory introduces substantial redundancy and
is ill-suited for population-based EAs. To address this challenge,
we propose an innovative meta-prompt for AOS, integrating three
key types of optimization information: optimization state, opera-
tor credit assignment, and similar experiences, to more effectively
guide LLMs in achieving dynamic operator selection.
The optimization state typically comprises the current popu-
lation’s status information and individual characteristics, effec-
tively reflecting the quality of the current solutions. Therefore, it is
commonly employed in constructing the state space of MDP mod-
els within state-based AOS frameworks. Yi et al. [59] categorized
optimization states into three types: search-dependent, solution-
dependent, and instance-dependent features. As shown in Table 1,
this study introduces six search-dependent features (𝑓1–𝑓6) and two
solution-dependent features (𝑓7, 𝑓8) to define the optimization state.
Notably, instance-dependent features are excluded in this study as
they rely on problem-specific characteristics, such as the number
of cities in TSP or vehicle capacity in VRP. Since this study aims
to create a general framework applicable to both numerical and
combinatorial optimization problems, instance-dependent features
are not considered due to their lack of generality.

3.3
Dual-Layer Experience Replay
In recent years, the effective utilization of optimization experience
to assist decision-making and enhance optimization performance in
AOS has attracted widespread attention. Aydin et al. [3] highlighted
the promising potential of offline experience when solving identical
problem instances. Pei et al. [42] achieved notable experimental
outcomes by treating different instances as offline experience in
a state-based AOS approach and balancing the results with the
stateless AOS method. In this study, we introduce the concept of
the experience replay mechanism from reinforcement learning to
facilitate the retrieval of optimization experience for LLMs. We

4
EXPERIMENTS
4.1
Experimental settings
Tasks and Datasets. Our experiments address two categories of
optimization tasks: real-valued optimization problems and classical
combinatorial optimization problems. For real-valued optimization,
we adopt three benchmark functions from the BBOB suite [20]: the
Sphere, Rastrigin, and Katsuura. Each function is evaluated under
5, 10, and 20-dimensional configurations.
For combinatorial optimization, we focus on three representa-
tive problem classes: Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), Job Shop
Scheduling (JSP), and Weapon-Target Assignment (WTA). Specifi-
cally, in TSP, we utilize cluster-based node distributions (as opposed
to uniform distributions) to simulate real-world scenarios [33]. As
an illustration, clu8@2 denotes 8 cities clustered around 2 central
points, with experiments covering three scales: clu8@2, clu15@3,
and clu30@5. For JSP, we construct instances based on standard
benchmarks. For instance, ft06@6 refers to a scheduling problem
with 6 jobs on 6 machines. Our evaluation includes three configu-
rations: ft06@6, ft10@10, and ft20@5 [5]. In WTA [28], to prevent
excessive resource concentration on limited targets, we impose a
constraint on allocation effectiveness (requiring the effectiveness of
each target to exceed 0.5). Instances follow a weapons@targets nam-
ing convention. For example, 9w@3 indicates allocating 9 weapons
to 3 targets. We perform experiments spanning 9w@3, 15w@4, and
25w@5 to ensure escalating complexity.

Random policy uniformly selects operators with equal probability.

Implementation Details. For real-valued optimization, we
employ a DE algorithm with a pool of four mutation strategies:
rand/1, rand/2, rand-to-best/2, and curr-to-rand/1. The parameters
are set to a crossover rate of 1.0 and a scaling factor of 0.5 (aligned
with configurations in [30, 49]). For combinatorial optimization, TSP
and JSP utilize a GA with legality-preserving crossover operators

efficiency of LAOS, this study conducts runtime comparisons across
representative benchmark instances, as summarized in Table 4. Ex-

costs and optimization benefits. When applied to low-cost optimiza-

substantially diminishes its performance advantages. Conversely,
in expensive optimization scenarios where single fitness evalua-

intensive domains. By demonstrating significant optimization gains

realized and operationalized.
5
CONCLUSIONS
In this study, we propose LAOS, a training-free LLM-driven frame-
work for online adaptive operator selection, which unifies stateless
and state-based optimization through three innovations. First, it
dynamically encodes state-space features, such as optimization
progress and population diversity, into structured prompts, allow-
ing the LLM to dynamically perceive the evolution of the search
landscape. Second, a credit assignment mechanism quantifies op-
erators’ historical performance, enhancing decision transparency.
Third, a dual-layer replay buffer combines offline historical storage
with online dynamic experience accumulation, strategically sam-
pling contextually relevant data to mitigate prompt redundancy.
Experiments demonstrate LAOS’s superior convergence and so-
lution quality in continuous/combinatorial optimization. Future
directions include: 1) Quantitative metrics for AOS decision-making
under dynamics; 2) Multi-objective LAOS with trade-off balancing;
3) Compact state representations for high-dimension problems.
